::: {#rem-score-name}
#### Why the score function is called "score"

Statisticians call the [score function](#def-score) by that name
because of its origin in genetics.
@fisher1935linkage gave each family in a study of linkage a "score", <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
which summarized what the family showed about the linkage parameter.
He compared that scoring rule with an "ideal score",
the [derivative](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-derivatives.html#def-derivative)
of the [log](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm) of the [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) of the data
as the linkage parameter varies,
which is the score function of these notes
[@wikipedia_informant_function].
For [independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-indpt) [observations](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-observation),
the [log-likelihood](#def-loglik) is a [sum](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-sums.html#def-summation) with one contribution from each of them,
so its derivative is also a sum.
@rao1948large, who had worked on estimating linkage parameters in Fisher's genetics laboratory,
based a test on the score function,
with one score for each parameter,
and called it a score test [@bera2024score].
The name then spread to the derivative itself.

In other settings, "score" refers to a different quantity.
These notes call a classifier's raw output the [log-odds](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-log-odds), never a "score",
so that "score" always refers to the derivative of the log-likelihood.
:::
